citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface and $m\ge1$. Give $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ its usual complex charts of elementary symmetric coordinates in disjoint support disks. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient and $p_i:\Sigma^m\to\Sigma$ its factor projections. For $i<j$ let $\Delta_{ij}=\{z_i=z_j\}$, and put $R=\sum_{i<j}\Delta_{ij}$, with coefficient one on every pair diagonal, including at their intersections. Then there is a holomorphic line-bundle isomorphism
$$q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\cong\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^m p_i^*T\Sigma\right)\otimes\mathcal O(R).$$
Under this isomorphism the holomorphic section $\det(dq)$ of
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}\left(\bigotimes_i p_i^*T\Sigma,q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\right)$$
corresponds to the canonical divisor section of $\mathcal O(R)$. In particular its zero divisor is exactly $R$, even at tuples with three or more equal entries; no transverse-intersection or simple-branch hypothesis is needed for the bundle identity.

Here $\mathcal O(R)$ is constructed by the actual local defining functions in the proof. For a smooth map $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):C\to\Sigma^m$ from a closed oriented surface with supplied finite smooth triangle data, the identity implies the degree formula
$$\deg\bigl((qF)^*\det(TX)\bigr)=\sum_i\deg(f_i^*T\Sigma)+\sum_{i<j}\deg\bigl((f_i,f_j)^*\mathcal O(\Delta)\bigr),$$
where $\Delta\subset\Sigma\times\Sigma$ is the ordinary diagonal. Degree means the finite face-winding degree of a complex line bundle. Whenever a pulled-back diagonal section has finitely many isolated zeros, its degree is the sum of their signed local winding indices; at a transverse coincidence this is the sign of $d(f_i-f_j)$ in an oriented surface coordinate. Degrees remain defined if two maps coincide identically.

For $m=1$ the empty divisor has its trivial line and constant section one; $q$ is the identity. For $m=0$ all determinants and tensor products over the one-point symmetric product are trivial and the degree formula is zero. This result does not identify the diagonal class in surface cohomology, compute a sphere's degree, prove a Maslov/domain formula, or realize arbitrary Whitney classes by incidence covers.

Assume Countable Choice. Supply a closed oriented smooth surface $\Sigma$ with an orientation-compatible finite polygon presentation whose paired boundary word is $\prod_{r=1}^h A_rB_rA_r^{-1}B_r^{-1}$, or the sphere presentation when $h=0$. This presentation includes its quotient map and finite subdivision into smooth face pieces; no surface classification theorem is assumed. Let $\Delta\subset\Sigma\times\Sigma$ be the complex diagonal for any compatible Riemann surface structure, and let $\mathcal O(\Delta)$ have its usual coordinate-difference section.

There are continuous circle-valued maps $a_r,b_r:\Sigma\to S^1$ with edge degrees dual to the ordered side loops. Write the same letters for their pulled-back integral degree-one circle classes, and $\omega$ for the positive degree-two face class. Their products satisfy $a_r\smile b_s=\delta_{rs}\omega$, $b_r\smile a_s=-\delta_{rs}\omega$, and all $a_ra_s,b_rb_s$ products vanish. For every pair of smooth maps $f,g:C\to\Sigma$ from a closed oriented surface with supplied finite triangle data,
$$\deg((f,g)^*\mathcal O(\Delta))=\deg f+\deg g-\sum_{r=1}^h\left\langle f^*a_r\smile g^*b_r-f^*b_r\smile g^*a_r,[C]\right\rangle.$$
Degrees of line bundles use finite face winding; map degree uses the positive polygon face generator, or equivalently signed inverse images of a regular value. In particular
$$\deg(f^*T\Sigma)=(2-2h)\deg f.$$
The formula permits $f=g$ or constant maps and does not interpret a nonisolated coincidence set as a finite transverse count. The supplied polygon is essential input to this choice-safe statement. No arbitrary-surface polygonal normal form, universal coefficient theorem or general Kunneth theorem is imported.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface, $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ with its standard complex structure, and $m\ge1$. For $a\in\Sigma$ put $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. This is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at repeated tuples. The universal incidence hypersurface $\mathcal E=\{(a,D):D\in E_a\}\subset\Sigma\times X$ carries a smooth complex divisor line bundle with its canonical section, whose zero set is $\mathcal E$ with multiplicity one.

For a smooth map $v:S\to X$, where $S$ is an oriented sphere or a closed disk, define $n_a(v)$ as the degree of the pullback point-divisor line bundle; for a disk use the canonical section to trivialize it on the boundary, and require $v(\partial S)\cap E_a=\varnothing$. The proof constructs this integer by elementary frame winding. It is defined even when a sphere lies wholly in $E_a$.

For a sphere, $n_a(v)$ is independent of $a$ on all of $\Sigma$. For a disk whose boundary tuples have all entries in a finite union of curves $\Gamma\subset\Sigma$, it is independent of $a$ on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$. If $v^{-1}(E_a)$ is finite and the map is holomorphic on a neighborhood of every one of these points, then
$$n_a(v)=\sum_{z\in v^{-1}(E_a)}\operatorname{ord}_z(F_a\circ v)\ge0,$$
where $F_a$ is any local holomorphic defining function of the smooth hypersurface $E_a$. Each term is a positive integer. Thus the degree agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity, while divisor containment is handled by its degree definition and actual point movement rather than an unsupported proper-intersection assumption.

Assume countable choice. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold with a smooth path $J_t$ of almost complex structures, and let $L_0,L_1$ be compact submanifolds totally real for $J_0,J_1$, respectively. Suppose their intersection is finite and transverse. At each intersection point choose a target chart in which $L_0=\mathbb R^m$, $L_1=i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t=i$ for every $t$. Retain those same charts and structures throughout.

A smooth fixed-end representative from $x$ to $y$ is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ with boundary on $L_0,L_1$, identically $x$ on one full negative tail and identically $y$ on one full positive tail. Its covariant Cauchy–Riemann linearization on fixed-end $H^1\to L^2$ spaces is Fredholm. Its real index is independent of the chosen smooth connection and of the representative under any smooth relative homotopy $H(h,s,t)$ with those boundary conditions, fixed endpoints, and one common pair of constant tails for all $h\in[0,1]$.

These indices add under concatenating two such representatives at their common endpoint, are zero for a constant representative, and change sign when $u(s,t)$ is replaced by $u(-s,t)$. Thus they define an integer index on smooth fixed-end representatives modulo the stated smooth relative homotopies, with concatenation and reversal laws. This result includes nonholomorphic representatives. It does not assume that a nonlinear moduli space exists or is regular.

A further relative smoothing and end-flattening argument is required to identify this smooth quotient with a Whitney-class set defined initially by arbitrary continuous disk maps and continuous relative homotopies. No such identification, domain Euler formula, or arbitrary-class representativity theorem is asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds. Then the critical value
set of $F$ is a null subset of $N$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

derivations.claim: We first construct an ordered lift after a harmless smooth homotopy; no holomorphic representative is assumed. The multiplicity partitions of $m$ stratify $X$ into finitely many smooth complex submanifolds. A partition with $r$ distinct support points has complex codimension $m-r$, as seen in the product coefficient charts. All strata except the distinct-root stratum and the single-double-root stratum have real codimension at least four. In finitely many target coordinate neighborhoods of the compact sphere image choose finitely many supported coordinate vector fields spanning its tangent fibers. Compose their small flows to vary the sphere; the parameter derivative at zero spans every target tangent space, and compactness preserves this spanning on one common small parameter ball. Thus its universal evaluation is a submersion. By [F5] a parameter arbitrarily close to zero makes the sphere transverse to every partition stratum. The resulting homotopic smooth map $u'$ misses all codimension-at-least-four strata and meets the simple-double-root stratum transversely in finitely many points $B$. Finiteness follows because the full repeated-point locus is closed, the higher strata are missed by the compact image, and its preimage is then a compact zero-dimensional manifold. The flow homotopy changes neither determinant-line degree nor point-divisor degree, using finite bundle frames over the compact parameterized sphere. [F1, F3, F5, F6, given, construct]

Over $S^2\setminus B$ take the finite set of all $m!$ orderings of the distinct tuple $u'(x)$. Locally its simple roots vary smoothly, so this set is an actual unbranched degree-$d$ covering with $d=m!$ and ordered map $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$; it may be disconnected. Near a point of $B$, the target coefficient chart has one colliding pair. Its quadratic discriminant $a$ is a complex normal coordinate to that stratum, and $a\circ u'$ has invertible real derivative. Complete this to a small source chart; all other roots and the colliding pair's center are smooth functions there. The monodromy exchanges just those two roots. Fill each two-cycle of ordered sheets by a disk: if $a\circ u'$ preserves orientation, set $a\circ u'\circ\pi=\zeta^2$; if it reverses orientation, set it equal to $\overline{\zeta}^{2}$. In both cases $\pi$ is an orientation-preserving smooth branched covering, and the ordered roots are the smooth center plus or minus $\zeta/2$ or $\overline{\zeta}/2$, with any fixed quadratic normalization absorbed into the coordinate. Unchanged labels give the same fill on their respective ordered sheets. This constructs a compact oriented surface $C$, smooth maps $f_i:C\to\Sigma$, and a degree-$d$ branched map $\pi:C\to S^2$ such that $qF=u'\pi$. There are finitely many filled disks. Cutting the punctured base sphere by finitely many arcs from its branch disks to one outer disk gives finitely many ordinary sheet polygons; lift and reglue those polygons and the power-coordinate filling sectors. Finite subdivisions give actual smooth face data for $C$. Thus [F1]–[F2] apply to this lift, without a general surface classification or an assumed incidence normalization theorem. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Put $N=\sum_i\deg f_i$, summed over all components of $C$. Choose a point $p\in\Sigma$ which is a regular value of all nonconstant $f_i$, misses every constant component value, and misses the finite support of $u'(B)$. Such a point exists by [F5]: the finite critical-value union is null and the additional excluded set is finite. In local tuple coordinates the canonical point-divisor equation is the product of its root coordinates minus $p$. Consequently the actual line identity $q^*\mathcal O(E_p)=\bigotimes_i p_i^*\mathcal O(p)$ holds: the local product definers have exactly the product transition units, as in [F1]'s divisor construction. Pulling back gives degree $N$, since each root's transverse inverse points have their signed local degrees. On the other hand $qF=u'\pi$, and pulling back a line on an oriented degree-$d$ branched covering multiplies its degree by $d$. This follows by choosing a graph and faces whose small degree-counting disks miss the finitely many branch values: each has $d$ orientation-positive lifts and all internal edges cancel. Hence $N=d\,n_p(u')=d\,n_z(u)$ by [F3] and step1.1. None of these signed degree equalities requires the sphere or root maps to be holomorphic. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

The ordered lift has a vanishing trace in every circle direction of [F2]. For any continuous $a:\Sigma\to S^1$, define $A:X\to S^1$ by $A(z_1+\cdots+z_m)=\prod_i a(z_i)$. This is continuous because the product on $\Sigma^m$ is symmetric and $q$ is the quotient map. The composite $A u':S^2\to S^1$ has a continuous real logarithm. An explicit choice-free argument is to lift it on each of two slightly enlarged closed hemispherical disks: a continuous circle map on a disk has a logarithm by subdividing each radial segment into one common number of short-argument increments, supplied by uniform continuity. Sum those increments from the disk center; the formula is continuous and exponentiates to the map. On the connected annular overlap the two logarithms differ by a constant integer multiple of $2\pi$, so adjust one to glue them. Therefore $A u'\pi=\prod_i af_i$ also has a logarithm. Its circle class is zero, while the class of a product is the sum of its factors' classes: the path-increment cocycles of [F2] differ only by the coboundary of the principal argument corrections. For $\alpha_{ir}=f_i^*a_r$ and $\beta_{ir}=f_i^*b_r$ this proves $\sum_i\alpha_{ir}=\sum_i\beta_{ir}=0$ in degree-one cohomology of $C$, for each $r$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Apply [F2] to every pair $f_i,f_j$. The sum of the first two terms of its diagonal formula is $(m-1)N$. For its cup correction, graded commutativity makes $\alpha_{ir}\smile\beta_{jr}-\beta_{ir}\smile\alpha_{jr}=\alpha_{ir}\smile\beta_{jr}+\alpha_{jr}\smile\beta_{ir}$. Summing over $i<j$ therefore gives $$(\sum_i\alpha_{ir})\smile(\sum_i\beta_{ir})-\sum_i\alpha_{ir}\smile\beta_{ir}=-\sum_i f_i^*(a_r\smile b_r).$$ Its evaluation is $-N$ by the positive polygon cup pairing and degree naturality in [F2]. Summing over $r$ gives correction $-hN$, so $$\sum_{i<j}\deg((f_i,f_j)^*\mathcal O(\Delta))=(m-1+h)N.$$ Also [F2] gives $\sum_i\deg(f_i^*T\Sigma)=(2-2h)N$. Now [F1] yields $$d\,\deg(u'^*\det(TX))=(2-2h)N+(m-1+h)N=(m+1-h)N.$$ Use step3.1 and divide by the positive integer $d$. Homotopy invariance from step1.1 gives the asserted identity for the original arbitrary sphere $u$, including negative degree and constant maps. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

A homotopy of complex structures identifies their determinant lines over the parameterized sphere. In detail, embed the finite family of bundle charts complex linearly in one finite trivial bundle by a finite partition, and use the continuous image projections. Uniform continuity allows finitely many parameter subdivisions on which consecutive projections differ by less than $1/2$; their restrictions are fiber isomorphisms. Their finite product identifies the two end complex bundles and hence the determinant degrees. This proves the asserted homotopic-complex-structure invariance, in particular for an explicitly supplied nearly-symmetric-to-standard homotopy; no assertion that arbitrary almost complex structures lie in that homotopy class is being made. [F1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Finally compare the actual relative determinant windings in [F4]. Flatten a small interior disk of the Whitney model to its attaching value, and flatten a small disk about the sphere attaching point, by relative coordinate homotopies; include the specified attaching path by a thin cylinder with a trivial bundle frame. Frame the determinant line on the flattened Whitney core, and on the sphere minus its attaching disk. On their common attaching circle the two sphere frames have transition loop of winding $c=\deg(u^*\det(TX))$, with the positive sphere orientation. Interior connected sum removes the attaching disks and glues their oppositely oriented circles. Extending the Whitney core frame over the inserted punctured sphere transfers precisely that transition of winding $c$ to the determinant trivialization along the physical boundary. This sign can be checked directly by face winding: all inner boundary contributions cancel except the positive sphere-face winding, so the relative determinant degree increases by $c$. The boundary Maslov phase in [F4] is the SQUARE of the complex determinant phase and hence increases by $2c$. The fixed end caps and physical boundary real planes have not changed. The actual Fredholm index formula of [F4] consequently gives $\mu(\phi\#u)-\mu(\phi)=2c$. Applying step4.1 and $m+1-h=k$ proves the claimed multipointed shift. The argument supplies the spherical correction only; it asserts neither the full nonspherical domain formula nor a boundary-disk count or normalized absolute grading. [F4, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes nonempty sphere and closed surface, with m>=1.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 4.1 include constant sphere maps and zero degree; generic homotopy handles initially wholly diagonal or contained-divisor maps.
Statement and step 2.1 include m=1 with trivial ordered cover and empty collision set.
Step 1.1 starts with arbitrary degenerate smooth sphere maps and homotopes them before using transversality; original degree is retained.
Step 6.1 retains physical strip boundary, fixed end caps and attaching path while changing the interior sphere class.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1 use genuine CC finite-dimensional Sard/transversality; the polygon and all subsequent covers/cells are finite.

boundaries.reason: This is a degree/index formula, not an equivalence.
